Inventory multiplicity

Source: R/multiplicity.inventory.R
multiplicity.inventory.Rd

Computes inventory multiplicity \(^{q}M\), the within-cluster diversity component under Hill-number partitioning, for every sample. It summarizes the average diversity inside clusters given element abundances and their cluster memberships. Use q to control abundance weighting (e.g., q = 0 richness-like, q = 1 Shannon-type).

Usage

multiplicity.inventory(abund, clust, q = 1)

Arguments

abund

Numeric matrix, data.frame or sparse Matrix of abundances with samples in rows and subunits in columns. Column names are the subunit identifiers.

clust

Vector or factor of cluster memberships for each subunit. If named, names are subunit identifiers and every column of abund must be listed; otherwise it must follow the columns of abund. A data frame is also accepted, with two columns (subunit identifiers, units) or one column of units (named by its row names, if set).

q

Numeric order of the Hill number (default 1). Controls abundance weighting:

q = 0

Richness-like weighting (all elements weighted equally)

q = 1

Shannon-type weighting (default, proportional to abundance)

q = 2

Simpson-type weighting (emphasizes abundant elements)

Must be non-negative.

Value

Named numeric vector with the inventory multiplicity \(^{q}M\) of every sample. This value can be interpreted as the effective number of equally abundant elements per cluster. A value of 1 indicates each cluster contains essentially one element (no diversity lost), while higher values indicate greater intra-cluster diversity. Samples with zero total abundance get 0. Since the index is otherwise at least 1, 0 flags an empty sample rather than a diversity value.

Details

Subunits with zero abundance in a sample are ignored for that sample.

References

  • Hill MO (1973) Diversity and evenness: a unifying notation and its consequences. Ecology 54(2):427-432. doi:10.2307/1934352

  • Jost L (2007) Partitioning diversity into independent alpha and beta components. Ecology 88(10):2427-2439. doi:10.1890/06-1736.1

See also

multiplicity.distance() for distance-based multiplicity, diversity.functional() for functional diversity indices

Examples

# Three clusters with three subunits each (a, b, c)
clust <- c(a1 = "a", a2 = "a", a3 = "a", b1 = "b", b2 = "b", b3 = "b",
           c1 = "c", c2 = "c", c3 = "c")
abund <- rbind(
  High = rep(10, 9),                     # every subunit equally abundant
  Low = c(10, 0, 0, 20, 0, 0, 30, 0, 0), # one subunit per cluster
  Uneven = c(10, 5, 2, 8, 8, 8, 20, 1, 0)
)
colnames(abund) <- names(clust)

multiplicity.inventory(abund, clust)          # High: 3, Low: 1
#>     High      Low   Uneven 
#> 3.000000 1.000000 2.103125 
multiplicity.inventory(abund, clust, q = 0)  # Richness-like
#>     High      Low   Uneven 
#> 3.000000 1.000000 2.666667 
multiplicity.inventory(abund, clust, q = 2)  # Simpson-type
#>     High      Low   Uneven 
#> 3.000000 1.000000 1.808864
